title: Steadfast Update II - Rewriting ASTs
excerpt: In the last Steadfast update I discussed the foundations of the project, its general API design, and my work on implementing the basic capacity of turning ASTs back to source code. In this update I'm discussing a new tool for rewriting Ruby ASTs.
content_html:
22·11·2026

Steadfast is a new Ruby project that aims to provide a new way to dynamically generate Ruby code at runtime by synthesizing and manipulating ASTs, as an alternative to the common technique of calling eval with a dynamically generated string containing Ruby source code.

In the last Steadfast update I discussed the foundations of the project, its general API design, and my work on implementing the basic capacity of turning ASTs back to source code (using Steadfast.to_source), as well as providing some facilities for translating backtrace locations for code derived from AST that were composed of pieces of code from different locations.

Over the last few days, I’ve concentrated on implementing the ability to transform an existing AST by replacing specific nodes therein. Previously, I called this “mutating” an AST, but actually I realized this term might be confusing, since Prism ASTs are inherently immutable, that is, they cannot be modified. Instead, you need to create a copy of an AST node with the requisite changes, so using the verb “mutate” is in fact incorrect. So henceforth I’ll use the term “rewrite” instead, which seems more fitting, since we’re basically taking existing code and rewriting it.

So, if Prism nodes are immutable, how can we rewrite them? Basically, Prism lets us create a copy of a given node, with specific attributes assigned new values:

node.copy(foo: some_value)

Now, there are some interesting nuances to this, because Prism nodes basically have three different kinds of attributes:

  • Child nodes - those are references to sub nodes. For example, a CallNode, representing a method call, will have a receiver subnode, that refers to the method receiver.
  • Plain value attributes - those are attributes that describe metadata associated with the node. For example, a CallNode will have a name attribute, whose value is a symbol, representing the name of the method to call.
  • Location attributes - those are references to Prism::Location instances that reference specific pieces of the source code syntax. For example, a CallNode will have a call_operator_loc attribute that references the . character for method calls with receivers. It will also reference the respective locations of the open and close parens, if the method call uses them.

That last group of node attributes, locations, is actually what Steadfast uses in order to convert a given AST back to a string containing Ruby code. So, if we want to rewrite a given node, we can’t just create a copy of it with its plain value attributes changed. For example, if we have a method call foo, which we want to change to bar, we can’t just rewrite the corresponding CallNode with a modified name attribute, because the location attribute for this (called message_loc) will still point to the original source code containing the string foo. We actually need to replace the CallNode with a another CallNode that actually represents a call to bar.

That means that we need to be able to synthesize that node. Here’s how this might be done:

def make_call_node(name)
  l = eval("-> { #{name} }")
  # Extract the first statement in the lambda body
  Steadfast.to_ast(l).body.body[0]
end

We can then proceed to replace the call_node

# the original code:
l = -> { foo }

l_ast = Steadfast.to_ast(l)
body_node = l_ast.body

rewritten_body_node = body_node.copy(body: [make_call_node(:bar)])
rewritten_ast = l_ast.copy(body: rewritten_body_node)

rewritten_lambda = eval(Steadfast.to_source(rewritten_ast))

In the above example, we acquire the lambda AST, then we get its body, create a copy of it containing the synthesized call to bar, and create a copy of the original AST, with the rewritten body.

As you can see, this is not very convenient. We need to reach into the AST to extract the body of the lambda, which is a StatementsNode, and we then need to inject the replacement method call into it. Once the body is rewritten, we need to create a copy of the lambda node itself, so it will point to the new body.

In the above example, we just needed to touch the body node, which is a subnode of the lambda root node, but in other cases we might need to drill down and make changes to some subnodes that are nested a lot deeper in the AST, which means that for any node that was replaced, we also need to replace all its parent nodes.

So this is what I set out to solve with Steadfast.rewrite. The implementation is quite simple: for any modification (rewrite) of a subnode, we automatically create modified copies of all its parent right up to the root. That’s why Steadfast.rewrite trakes an AST as its first argument, and returns a rewritten AST as its return value.

To show how Steadfast.rewrite can be used, let’s look at two possible applications of this technique:

Example 1: Tail Call Optimization

In the previous update, I discussed a possible way to do tail call optimization by rewriting an AST. Take for example a recursive factorial method:

def fact(n, acc = 1)
  return acc if n <= 1

  fact(n - 1, n * acc)
end

We can do tail call optimization by rewriting it as follows:

def fact(n, acc = 1)
  loop do
    return acc if n <= 1

    n, acc = [n - 1, n * acc]
  end
end

Basically, we rewrite the method by putting everything in a loop, and replacing the tail call with a multiple local variable assignment. Here’s how we can do it using Steadfast.rewrite:

def rewrite_with_tail_call(meth)
  ast = Steadfast.to_ast(meth)
  params = ast.parameters
  *body, tail = ast.body.body

  body2 = make_loop(*body, convert_tail_call(tail, params))
  ast2 = Steadfast.rewrite(ast, ast.body => { body: body2 })
  eval(Steadfast.to_source(ast2))
end

The method above extracts the AST for the given method, separates the method body into a body (containing all statements but the tail), and a tail which references the last statement. We then synthesize a loop node containing the body and the converted tail, and call Steadfast.rewrite to replace the original body with the loop. Finally, we call eval with the rewritten source code, which effectively redefines the method. Here’s how we make the loop node:

def make_loop(*statements)
  l = eval("-> { loop do; 1; end }")
  loop_node = Steadfast.to_ast(l).body.body[0]
  loop_block_body = loop_node.block.body
  Steadfast.rewrite(loop_node, loop_block_body => { body: statements })
end

We synthesize a call to loop, and then use Steadfast.rewrite to inject the given list of statements into its body. To convert the tail call, we use a similar technique:

def convert_tail_call(tail, params)
  make_multi_write_node(
    [*params.requireds.map(&:name), *params.optionals.map(&:name)],
    tail.arguments.arguments
  )
end

def make_multi_write_node(names, values)
  l = eval("-> { #{names.join(', ')} = [nil] }")
  multi_write_node = Steadfast.to_ast(l).body.body[0]
  Steadfast.rewrite(multi_write_node, multi_write_node.value => { elements: values })
end

We synthesize a multi-write node (representing assignment to multiple local variables) with the given variable names, and we use Steadfast.rewrite to inject the tail call arguments into the assignment as an array.

Example 2: Pipe Operator Implementation

A nifty feature of Elixir is the ability to use a pipe operator (|>) for putting data through a series of transformations. This does not really exist in Ruby, though you can use the somewhat unwieldy syntax .then { ... }. While method chaining is quite useful for many kinds of computations, sometimes you wish you had something like a pipe operator in Ruby, the idea being that at each step of the pipe, we inject the last return value as the first argument to the next method call. What if we could do something like the following:

pipe { 1 >> add(2) >> mul(3) >> pow(4) }

Since in Ruby, binary operators are implemented as method calls, but with a special syntax, the following is synonymous with the above:

pipe { 1.>>(add(2)).>>(mul(3)).>>(pow(4)) }

Interestingly, the AST representation of the code will have the call to pow at the top of the AST (that is, on the outside), with the preceding calls being expressed as the receiver of that method call, something like the following:

call(
  name: :>>,
  receiver: call(
    name: :>>,
    receiver: call(
      name: :>>,
      receiver: 1,
      arguments: [add(2)]
    ),
    arguments: [mul(3)]
  ),
  arguments: [pow(4)]
)

But this code is just an intent, it won’t acutally work since any of those calls to add, mul and pow needs to provide two arguments. We need to be able to transform this syntax into a sequence of method calls where the result of each method call is injected as an argument into the next one.

The rewrite operation we need to do is to flip the receiver and the argument for each call to >>, such that the argument becomes the method call, and the receiver is injected as an additional first argument into that method call, in order to achieve the following:

-> { pow(mul(add(4, 3), 6), 2) }

Here again, we can use Steadfast.rewrite to do just that:

l = -> { 1 >> add(2) >> mul(3) >> pow(4) }
l_ast = Steadfast.to_ast(l)
p_ast = Steadfast.rewrite(l_ast) { |n, &r|
  next n if !(n in Ruby::Prism::CallNode(name: :>>))

  call_node = n.arguments.arguments[0]
  next n if !n in Ruby::Prism::CallNode

  arguments = [Steadfast.rewrite(n.receiver, &r), call_node.arguments]
  Steadfast.rewrite(call_node, call_node.arguments => { arguments: })
}
p = eval(Steadfast.to_source(p_ast))

In this example, instead of providing Steadfast.rewrite with a list of specific node replacements, we give it a block that is invoked for each node in the AST. The block should return either a replacement node, or the original node, in which case no replacement is made.

In the rewriter block, we filter out anything that is not a call to >> (since in Ruby, binary operators are actually method calls). Notice how we use next n to tell Steadfast.rewrite that no replacement is made and that we want to continue visiting other nodes. We then extract the call_node to the right of the >> operator (its argument), and replace the operator call with this call node, with its arguments rewritten so as to inject the value to the left of the operator into the call.

Notice how we recursively call Steadfast.rewrite(n.receiver, &r). In order to make it possible for us to recurse inside the block, Steadfast.rewrite yields, along with the node, a reference to the block itself, which lets us call Steadfast.rewrite recursively with the same block. This technique is interesting in and of itself, and is quite useful as you can see, since working with ASTs is inherently recursive.

Pipe operator syntax transformation and tail call optimization are but two possible applications of AST rewriting, but Steadfast.rewrite can also be used for inlining method calls, and more generally, for such things as wrapping code in a loop, or in a begin/rescue block, unrolling loops, injecting arguments into method calls… the possibilities are endless!

In the upcoming stages of this project, I’ll use Steadfast.rewrite to implement the code quoting tool (aka quote/unquote), as well as for synthesizing different kinds of AST nodes.

The Steadfast.rewrite Implementation

The Steadfast.rewrite implementation is surprisigingly succint, about 35LOC. At the heart of it is the following method that visits each node in the AST:

def visit(node)
  node2 = @rewrite_block.(node, &@rewrite_block)
  return node2 if node2 != node

  changes = {}
  node.deconstruct_keys(nil).each do |k, v|
    if v.is_a?(Ruby::Prism::Node)
      v2 = visit(v)
      changes[k] = v2 if v2 != v
    elsif v in [Ruby::Prism::Node, *]
      v2 = v.map { visit(it) }
      changes[k] = v2 if v2 != v
    end
  end
  changes.empty? ? node : node.copy(**changes)
end

We start the visit by invoking the rewrite block with the given node. If a replacement node was returned by the block, we return it immediately. Otherwise, we dive into the node attributes (using deconstruct_keys), and visit each subnode, or array of subnodes. If any replacements were returned for any of the attributes, we make a copy of the node with the relevant changes. Thus we ensure that any replacement to a nested node will result in its parent being replaced as well, all the way up to the root of the AST.

To allow Steadfast.rewrite to be called with a hash of replacements instead of a visitor block, we do the following:

rewrite_block ||= ->(n) do
  if (v = replacements[n]) && v.is_a?(Hash)
    n.copy(**v)
  else
    replacements.key?(n) ? replacements[n] : n
  end
end

And that’s basically all there is to it - we have a general purpose tool for rewriting ASTs!

What’s Next for Steadfast

My plan for this coming week is to spend some time on creating tools for synthesizing different kinds of nodes more easily. We’ve seen some examples of this in the discussion above, for example:

def make_call_node(name)
  l = eval("-> { #{name} }")
  Steadfast.to_ast(l).body.body[0]
end

I already have some ideas about how this could be improved and generalized, and I also want to design an API that will be convenient to use, even for people who are less familiar with ASTs.

In addition, some more work should be done on being able to maintain correct backtraces for exceptions raised in code based on synthetic ASTs. This is definitely something on which I’m going to spend more time, and more tests.

blocks.html_en: That last group of node attributes, locations, is actually what Steadfast uses in order to convert a given AST back to a string containing Ruby code. So, if we want to rewrite a given node, we can’t just create a copy of it with its plain value attributes changed. For example, if we have a method call foo, which we want to change to bar, we can’t just rewrite the corresponding CallNode with a modified name attribute, because the location attribute for this (called message_loc) will still point to the original source code containing the string foo. We actually need to replace the CallNode with a another CallNode that actually represents a call to bar.

blocks.html_en: We start the visit by invoking the rewrite block with the given node. If a replacement node was returned by the block, we return it immediately. Otherwise, we dive into the node attributes (using deconstruct_keys), and visit each subnode, or array of subnodes. If any replacements were returned for any of the attributes, we make a copy of the node with the relevant changes. Thus we ensure that any replacement to a nested node will result in its parent being replaced as well, all the way up to the root of the AST.
